# Proof

## Conventions and the precise statement

**Relations.** For relations $R, S \subseteq X \times X$ we use the (ProofWiki) convention
$$S \circ R = \{(a,c) : \exists b \in X,\ (a,b) \in R \text{ and } (b,c) \in S\},$$
i.e. in $S \circ R$ the relation $R$ is applied first. Composition is associative, so $U_n = V_n \circ V_{n-1} \circ \cdots \circ V_1$ is well defined and
$$U_1 = V_1, \qquad U_{n+1} = V_{n+1} \circ U_n \quad (n \ge 1). \tag{1}$$
For $R \subseteq X\times X$ and $a \in X$, $R(a) = \{b \in X : (a,b) \in R\}$ is the image of $a$. $R$ is symmetric iff $(a,b)\in R \Rightarrow (b,a) \in R$. We write $y \prec x$ for $y \preccurlyeq x,\ y \neq x$. A well-ordering is a total ordering, so for $x \ne y$ exactly one of $y \prec x$, $x \prec y$ holds.

**Discreteness.** A set $\mathcal A$ of subsets of a topological space $X$ is *discrete* if every $z \in X$ has a neighbourhood $N$ meeting at most one element of $\mathcal A$. The statement assumes a topology on $X$ without giving one. As in the source context (Characterization of Paracompactness in $T_3$ Space), we take the $V_n$ to be neighbourhoods of the diagonal $\Delta_X$ in $X \times X$ (product topology). The only thing we actually use is the consequence

> (N) for all $m$ and all $z \in X$, the set $V_m(z)$ is a neighbourhood of $z$ in $X$.

*Proof of (N).* $V_m$ contains an open set $O \supseteq \Delta_X$. Since $(z,z) \in O$, there are open sets $G, H \subseteq X$ with $(z,z) \in G \times H \subseteq O$. Then $z \in H$, and for $h \in H$ we have $(z,h) \in G\times H \subseteq V_m$, i.e. $h \in V_m(z)$. So $z \in H \subseteq V_m(z)$ with $H$ open. $\square$

We shall prove the following purely set-theoretic statement, which uses no topology at all:

> **Key Lemma.** Let $n \ge 1$ and $z \in X$. If $x, y \in X$ are such that $V_{n+2}(z) \cap A_n(x) \ne \emptyset$ and $V_{n+2}(z) \cap A_n(y) \neq \emptyset$, then $x = y$.

## Proof of the Key Lemma

Suppose, for contradiction, that $x \ne y$, $p \in V_{n+2}(z) \cap A_n(y)$ and $q \in V_{n+2}(z)\cap A_n(x)$. The hypotheses are symmetric in $(x,q)$ and $(y,p)$, and $\preccurlyeq$ is total, so we may assume $y \prec x$.

1. $p \in V_{n+2}(z)$ gives $(z,p) \in V_{n+2}$. Because $V_{n+2}$ is symmetric (note $n+2>0$), $(p,z) \in V_{n+2}$.
2. $q \in V_{n+2}(z)$ gives $(z,q) \in V_{n+2}$.
3. From 1 and 2, $(p,q) \in V_{n+2}\circ V_{n+2} \subseteq V_{n+1}$ (the hypothesis with index $n+2 > 0$).
4. $p \in A_n(y) \subseteq U_n(y)$, so $(y,p) \in U_n$.
5. From 4 and 3, $(y,q) \in V_{n+1} \circ U_n = U_{n+1}$ by (1); i.e. $q \in U_{n+1}(y)$.
6. Since $y \preccurlyeq x$ and $y \neq x$, $U_{n+1}(y) \subseteq \bigcup_{w \prec x} U_{n+1}(w)$, so $q \notin A_n(x) = U_n(x) \setminus \bigcup_{w \prec x} U_{n+1}(w)$.

This contradicts $q \in A_n(x)$. Hence $x = y$. $\blacksquare$

## Conclusion

Fix $n \ge 1$ and $z \in X$. Put $N = V_{n+2}(z)$; by (N), $N$ is a neighbourhood of $z$. Suppose $N$ meets two elements $B, C$ of $\mathcal A_n$. By definition of $\mathcal A_n$, $B = A_n(x)$ and $C = A_n(y)$ for some $x, y \in X$. By the Key Lemma $x = y$, hence $B = C$. So $N$ meets at most one element of $\mathcal A_n$. Since $z$ was arbitrary, $\mathcal A_n$ is a discrete set of subsets of $X$, for every $n \in \N_{>0}$. $\blacksquare$

**Remarks.** (a) Suppose $p \in A_n(x) \cap A_n(y)$ and take $z = p$. Since $\Delta_X \subseteq V_{n+2}$, we have $p \in V_{n+2}(p)$, so the Key Lemma gives $x = y$. Hence the sets $A_n(x)$ with distinct indices $x$ are pairwise disjoint. (b) By the Key Lemma, $\mathcal A_n$ is discrete in *every* topology on $X$ for which (N) holds (it is "uniformly discrete" with respect to $V_{n+2}$). This is the only place the missing topological hypothesis is used.
